title: Pulp Fiction
prompt: Your client is the CEO of a major juice manufacturer. She is concerned about the company's profitability compared to other competitors'. She would like your assistance in identifying the reason behind this.

notes.title: Questions
items: What kind of juices does the company produce?
What are the other revenue streams?
Where does the company lie on the value chain?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Treat packaging as a raw material
Always clarify whether packaging is in-house
Supplier overcharging: check cost or margin

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Asking for the market share to rule out economies of scale

framework:
Candidate: Understood. I would like to know more about the manufacturer. What kind of juices do they produce? Are there any other revenue streams such as jams? Which geographies do they operate in? Where do we lie on the value chain.
Interviewer: For the purpose of this case, their only revenue stream is processed fruit juice that they sell across India. The company is involved in manufacturing and distribution. This is the case with our competitors as well.
Candidate: Okay. I would now like to understand the problem better. The client is concerned about the company's profitability. This could either mean that the company is making less sales compared to competitors or they are incurring higher costs per unit of sales.
Interviewer: Good question. For every Rs 100 of sales, our competitors incur Rs 75 as cost. Our company incurs Rs 78 for the same.
Candidate: Interesting. It is possible that we are a smaller company as compared to our competitors who may be enjoying the advantage of economies of scale. Do we have details as to the respective market shares of the major players in the market?
Interviewer: There are 5 major players in the market. We hold a 20% market share.
Candidate: That rules out my initial hypothesis as we have a sizeable market share. Since the problem is with the company's cost structure, I would like to benchmark our cost structure with our competitors'. The first step would be to identify the major costs incurred in the process of manufacturing and selling the juice and then analyse the amount incurred under each head.
Interviewer: Go ahead.
Candidate: The costs can be grouped into in-bound logistics, production, out-bound logistics and marketing. In-bound logistics can further be divided into raw materials and transportation of the materials to the production site. Production includes processing of the raw materials into juice and the subsequent packaging of the juice. Out-bound logistics include the storage and transportation of the juice and margins allowed to the resellers. Since I am not too familiar with the industry, it is possible that I have missed a few relevant costs.
Interviewer: You have covered all the major cost heads. We spend Rs. 3 more than our competitors on raw materials per Rs 100 of sales. Other costs are more or less equal.
Candidate: According to my knowledge, the raw materials used in fruit juices are fruit extract/pulp, sugar, preservatives and water. I would also like to know how the product is packed. Is the packaging done in-house? What about our competitors?
Interviewer: The juice is packaged in PET bottles. The preforms for the bottles are purchased. The preform is then heated in-house and blown into a bottle shape. Finally, the juice is filled into the bottles. Our competitors follow the same procedure.
Candidate: Okay, so our raw materials will include these preforms. Do we know which raw materials we are paying more for in comparison to our competitors?
Interviewer: In fact, we are paying extra for the preforms.
Candidate: The cost of preforms is determined by the following factors:
Cost of preforms = Number of preforms * Cost per preform
Candidate: Number of preforms may be higher because we may be packaging in smaller quantities or there is wastage. Alternatively, our suppliers may be charging us higher for the pre-forms.
Interviewer: We use the same suppliers as our competitors. However, they are charging us more for the pre-forms. Why do you think this is the case?
Candidate: That is strange. It is possible that the suppliers are incurring higher costs in producing our pre-forms due to special raw materials used or customisation required by our company. If not, they may be making higher margins from us due to lower negotiation power or contractual factors such as agreements for a shorter period.
Interviewer: Correct. Our company requires a different pre-form which is compatible with the machines we own. We can end the case here.

Pulp Fiction Framework & Recommendations
TURNAROUND STRATEGIES FOR A JUICE MANUFACTURER
Clarifying Questions: What kind of juices does the company produce? What are the other revenue streams?
Brownie Points: Asking for the market share to rule out economies of scale
Keep In Mind: Most variable costs can be broken down into Number of units * Cost/unit
RECOMMENDATIONS: Manufacture our own pre-forms after doing a cost-benefit analysis and confirming it is feasible to do so
Change our packaging machinery if this will ultimately lead to cost savings

title: Don't Steel From Us
prompt: Hey. Your client is a steel manufacturing company. You are required to diagnose why the company's costs have increased by 4% in the last 6 months.

notes.title: Questions
items: Different grades of steel?
Who the consumers are?
Where we lie on value chain?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Analyse contractor's per-km cost structure when transportation is outsourced
Identical below-cost rates signal contractor collusion

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Method of calculating distance between Jamshedpur and Delhi through prior air travel experience

visualisations.title: Variable Cost per km: Calculated vs. Contractor
rows: Salary Rs. 45,000/month; 5 round trips/month; 1,500 km one-way
visualisations.insight: Contractor charges Rs. 2.50/km less than calculated variable cost, which is the anomaly that signals collusion.

visualisations.title: Total Cost
visualisations.rhs: No. of Trucks × No. of km per Truck × Rate per km

derivations.rhs: Total Volume to be Transported ÷ (Volume per Truck per Trip × No. of Trips per Truck)
(Capacity per Truck × Percentage Utilised) - (Wastage + Theft + Loss)

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. I'd like to understand the problem a little better. Where is our client located? Where are their customers located? Which step of the value chain do they lie on? Do they have different grades of steel?
Interviewer: Our client is located in Jamshedpur. They transport steel to 4 locations - Agra, Delhi, Mumbai and Haryana. They manufacture the steel and then transport it to various customers, mainly building manufacturers. For the purpose of this case, assume they make only one type of steel.
Candidate: Great. Do we have any information on how competitors have fared in the last 6 months?
Interviewer: We do not have any information on that. You can proceed with your approach.
Candidate: Sure. I'd like to break down our total costs into Fixed and Variable costs. Under Fixed costs, I'd like to analyse costs incurred on Land, Interest payments, R&D (Since we manufacture steel), Machinery, Factories, Fixed Component of Labour and other assets owned. Under Variable costs, I'd like to analyse the various steps involved in the manufacturing of steel and isolate the problem. Do we know which amongst Fixed and Variable costs have increased?
Interviewer: Sure, Fixed costs have remained the same. Variable costs have increased.
Candidate: Okay. The various variable costs would be:
Value Chain = Cost of acquiring raw materials – Transportation of raw materials to factories – Processing cost (Includes labour and utilities such as electricity) – Storage costs – Packaging costs – Transportation of final product to consumers – Distribution costs – Marketing costs – Miscellaneous costs like tax and legal expenses
Are there any other costs I am missing?
Interviewer: No, you are not. The cost of transportation has increased for the client.
Candidate: Interesting. I'd like to analyse the logistics better. Can I assume transportation is done through trucks since that is the preferred mode in this industry?
Interviewer: You're right. We transport it through trucks.
Candidate: Do we own the trucks or do we outsource transportation? Also, have the costs of transportation gone up in all locations?
Interviewer: We do not own the trucks. We outsource the transportation. Costs have increased in our transportation to all locations.
Candidate: Since we outsource transportation, we must be paying a rate per km covered by the truck to the contractor and hence will not have to pay separately for fuel, driver or maintenance costs.
The total cost of transportation = Number of trucks * km covered per truck * Rate per km
Candidate: Do we know which of these has increased in the last 6 months?
Interviewer: Why don't you analyse the number of trucks first?
Candidate: Sure.
Total number of trucks required = (Total volume required to be transported)/(Volume transported by each truck per trip * Number of trips completed by each truck)
Where,
Volume transported by each truck per trip = (Total capacity of truck * % of capacity utilized) - (Wastage + Theft + Loss)
Candidate: Do we know which of these have changed?
Interviewer: Spot on. The % capacity utilized has gone down in the last 6 months. The contractor uses only one type of truck and the capacity utilized is low. Moving on to the Rate per km charged, the CEO has a hypothesis that we are being overcharged. Why don't you estimate the various variable costs the contractor incurs and compare this with the actual rate charged?
Candidate: Sure. I think there will primarily be 4 costs he incurs for every km travelled (Variable aspect):
1) Fuel costs
2) Driver and helper costs
3) Maintenance costs
4) Toll costs
_(Calculating distance)_
I know that the average flight time from Jamshedpur to Delhi is 2.5 hours. The average speed of a commercial plane is 600 kmph. This gives us an approximate distance of 1500 km between the two locations.
_(Calculating fuel costs)_
Cost of fuel/km = (Cost of fuel/litre)/(Number of km/litre)
Diesel prices hover around Rs 80/litre. Trucks give a mileage of about 8 km/litre. Thus, the cost of fuel is Rs 10/km.
_(Calculating driver & helper costs)_
Assuming around 5 round trips in a month (1 round trip takes about 6 days) and an average monthly salary of Rs. 25,000 and Rs. 20,000 for the driver and helper respectively:
Cost/km = (Salary for a month)/(Distance covered in a month)
= (Rs. 45,000)/(1,500 km * 5 * 2)
= Rs 3/km
_(Calculating maintenance costs)_
Assuming the truck is serviced once every 10 round trips and the average servicing cost is Rs. 30,000:
The maintenance cost/km = (Servicing costs)/(Distance covered per service)
= (Rs. 30,000)/(1500 km * 10 * 2)
= Rs 1/km
_(Calculating toll costs)_
Assuming a monthly toll pass across different borders costs Rs 7,500:
The toll cost/km = (Monthly Toll costs)/(Distance covered in a month)
= (Rs. 7,500)/(1500 km * 5 * 2)
= Rs 0.5/km
This brings our total cost/km to Rs. 14.50. What is the cost that the contractor charges us per km?
Interviewer: Brilliant job. He charges us Rs. 12/km. Can you analyse why this might be happening?
Candidate: That's interesting. Something seems to be fishy. I can think of two reasons -
1) Since he is not using his full capacity, he might be taking up additional contracts for shorter distance between Jamshedpur and Delhi, thereby increasing his revenues.
2) On the return journey his truck would be empty, the fuel costs might be much lower and hence the cost we arrived at might not be accurate.
Interviewer: Perfect. It has been found that the contractor takes up additional smaller contracts to fill the extra space in his trucks.
Candidate: Okay. My immediate suggestion would be to hire a new contractor as this would reduce the number of trucks required and bring down our total costs. I would like to know what the capacity utilization and rate per km of other contractors are?
Interviewer: In fact, all contractors in Jamshedpur have similar capacities and quantity utilizations. They all charge a similar rate of Rs. 12/km too.
Candidate: This leads me to believe that the contractors are colluding and all are conducting multiple contracts on their journey.
Interviewer: Spot on. You have identified the problem! You can give recommendations (next page) and quickly sum up the case. Thank you.

Don't Steel From Us Framework & Recommendations
INCREASING TRANSPORTATION COSTS OF A STEEL COMPANY
Clarifying Questions: Different grades of steel? Who the consumers are? Where we lie on value chain?
Brownie Points: Method of calculating distance between Jamshedpur and Delhi through prior air travel experience
Keep In Mind: When required, taking actual values to arrive at cost is important Make sure to never make a mistake while calculating as it is a sin
RECOMMENDATIONS: All steel manufacturing companies can come together to stop this practice of the contractors
The company can purchase its own trucks and transport steel on its own after a cost-benefit analysis
The company can pay a higher rate/km to negotiate an increase in capacity utilized, bringing down total cost as whole

framework:
Candidate: That's interesting. Can I assume the airline to be similar to Spice Jet? Also, does the airline operate both domestic and international flights? What are our other service offerings? Since it is a low-cost operator, can I assume there is only economy class?
Interviewer: Yes, it is similar to Spice Jet. For the purpose of this case, you can assume that the airline only operates domestic flights. They have a presence across the country. Yes, the operator only offers economy class.
Candidate: Alright. I would like to understand the decline in profitability a little better. Since when have we been facing this issue and what is the magnitude of decline? Have other airlines reported a similar drop? Is the issue specific to certain locations?
Interviewer: It is a marginal decline in profits and has been happening for a couple of months now. Other operators don't seem to be facing this issue. We are facing the decline across the country.
Candidate: It seems that the issue is only affecting our airline then. Interesting. Declining profits could be driven either by declining revenues or increasing costs. I would first like to break down revenues into
Revenues = Number of Flights * Number of Seats/Flight * Occupancy * Price/Ticket
and see if there's been a change in any of these factors over the last two months. This is the revenue from ticket sales. Other revenue streams would include value-added services, on-flight food and beverages, merchandise purchases and advertisements.
Interviewer: Fair enough. None of these factors have seen a significant change. What would you like to look at next?
Candidate: Okay. It is clear that revenues have not seen a decline. I would now like to look at the major cost drivers and benchmark them with our competitors. Once we identify which costs have seen a rise, we can dive deeper into why this has been happening.
Interviewer: Makes sense. What is your question?
Candidate: I would like to know if the increase has been in fixed costs or variable costs. Fixed costs include costs like lease fees paid for the carriers, airport charges (hangar, space for check-in counters, fee for boarding gates, etc), employee compensation and back-end administrative costs. Major variable costs would include cost of fuel, commission paid to airports, etc.
Interviewer: Great. There has been a significant increase in the amount we're paying for fuel. Why don't you analyse why this may be happening?
Candidate: Sure. Apart from flights, we may be needing fuel for our passenger buses and cargo trucks as well. Do we know where the increase has been?
Interviewer: Good question. Fuel consumption by flights has increased.
Candidate: The amount we are paying for fuel would be determined by
Cost of Fuel = Number of flights * Number of kilometres/flight * Number of litres/kilometre * Cost/litre + Cost of wastage
Candidate: Since the number of flights has not changed, my hypothesis is that number of kilometres/flight has seen an increase. It is unlikely that our mileage has changed in the last two months and any changes in fuel prices would have affected our competitors as well. Another possible reason would be an increase in wastage.
Interviewer: Excellent. The number of kilometres/flight has increased.
Candidate: I would like to analyse the flight path now. According to my personal experience, the plane first taxis to the runway. After this, the plane takes off upon reaching a suitable speed. Once it is airborne, the plane ascends until it reaches a point of stabilisation. Few hours later, we reach our destination and choose a landing point. Before descending, we circle the airport waiting for approval from the Air Traffic Control. After obtaining permission, we descend and touchdown. We finally decelerate and taxi to the drop point. Do we know at what stage our distance travelled has gone up?
Interviewer: You seem to know a lot about airlines! Perfect. Our circling time has increased.
Candidate: Interesting. There are three things I would like to analyse here. The Air Traffic Control may not be giving us clearance to land as promptly as before. It is also possible that we are picking up the signal late due to some faulty or outdated equipment in our planes. Lastly, I want to know if the time between receiving the signal and landing is longer than before due to the lack of expertise of our flight crew. My guess is that we are not facing this problem since our entire fleet is facing this problem.
Interviewer: Correct.
Candidate: Okay. This could be due to increase in air traffic during our landing times due to which waiting time has increased. It could also be the result of policy changes by the Airport Authorities where higher circling time is required. However, since we are the only airline facing the issue, I would like to know if other airlines are being favoured for some reason.
Interviewer: Spot on! Two months ago, the Airport Authority of India started a priority-based system wherein airlines paying a certain fee will be allowed to land first. The CEO is wondering if we should start doing the same. What would you recommend?

Interviewer: Makes sense. We can end the case here.

title: Beauty Lies On The Inside
prompt: Hey, let's begin with a quick case. Your client is Donatella Versace, owner of a famous retail apparel store in India. Due to Covid-19, profits of the store have decreased. To increase profits, she has decided to open a makeup outlet inside the store. She has approached you to decide whether this is a wise decision.

wise-decision.label: Is Opening a Makeup Outlet a Wise Decision?

notes.title: Questions

How much space is the makeup outlet going to take?
Why only makeup as an alternative?
In-house manufacturing or 3rd-party distribution?

notes.title: Keep In Mind

framework:
Candidate: Sure. I'd like to understand the problem better. Where is her store located? What are the products currently available at her store? Also, how much have profits fallen by in this period?
Interviewer: Her store is located in Delhi. She currently sells clothes for men and women. Profits have fallen by 15%.
Candidate: Interesting. Does she manufacture her own clothes or is she a 3rd party distributor? How much space inside the store is the makeup outlet going to take?
Interviewer: She is a distributor of clothes and plans to be for makeup as well. The makeup outlet is proposed to take up 20% of the space in the store.
Candidate: Lastly, is there any particular reason for choosing a makeup outlet or is our client open to other ideas as well?
Interviewer: She believes makeup products will sell much better post the pandemic period and hence, this is the only option she is considering.
Candidate: I can now begin. Since our client's objective is to increase profits, I shall evaluate this decision on the basis of the additional revenues she will earn minus the additional costs she will incur.
Interviewer: Sure, sounds good,
Candidate: Therefore, if - Additional Revenues > Additional Costs, this is a wise decision.
In additional costs, I would like to incorporate not just the costs of setting up and buying the products, but also the revenue foregone from the lost retail apparel space, since this is an opportunity cost.
Interviewer: Brilliant. Opportunity costs become a major consideration. Why don't you find the breakeven point of sales for this decision in a month? What is the data you would require?
Candidate: Sure, I know that
Breakeven point of sale = (Fixed cost)/(Sale price - Variable cost)
Therefore, I would require the following information:
1) Fixed costs involved in setting up the makeup outlet
2) Opportunity cost of sales foregone
3) Average sale price of a makeup product
4) Average cost price of purchasing a makeup item
5) Other variable costs involved (Staff, etc.)
Interviewer: That seems comprehensive. You may note down the following information:
Interviewer: Cost incurred to change the layout and set up the various aspects of the outlet - Rs. 40,000. The entire outlet has an area of 10,000 sq. ft and earns a profit of Rs. 25,000 a day. Assume that every part of the store contributes equally to profits. Average sale price of a makeup item would be around Rs. 1,000 and the average cost price would be Rs. 400. The other variable costs per product would come up to Rs. 100.
Candidate: Great! Since the costs have been given to us in terms of a one-time fixed expenditure and a daily opportunity cost; we will first find the break-even point where we will be able to recover the fixed cost incurred. Subsequently, we will calculate the number of products we will need to sell daily in order to experience an incremental profit.
_(Calculating daily opportunity cost)_
If income is uniform, then every 1 sq. ft of the apparel segment contributes Rs 2.5 (Rs. 25,000/10,000). Since the makeup division is expected to take up 2000 sq. ft, the revenue lost would be equal to
2000 Sq. ft x Rs 2.5 = Rs. 5,000 per day
Thus, total cost to be recovered = Rs. 40,000. Rs. 5,000 everyday the store is open is the opportunity cost.
_(Calculation on next page)_
Thus, we realise that we need to sell 80 items on an average from our makeup outlet to recover the fixed cost of renovations and we need to sell 10 products daily to recover the opportunity cost of giving up on 20% of the apparel segment.
Interviewer: Brilliant! You have correctly identified the amount. Let's finally move on to recommendations on how we can further improve the sale from our makeup outlet.
Candidate: I can think of the following suggestions -
1) Online presence: Ensuring we have a website that provides for checking on stock availability and delivery option.
2) Tie-ups with e-commerce aggregators: Presence on sites like Flipkart and Amazon can also add to sales.
3) Range of makeup products not delimited to women: Keeping in mind the increasing trend of makeup for men and LGBTQi+ community
4) Creating special ranges for all income segments and demographics
5) Tie-ups with micro-influencers on Instagram and other platforms
6) Discounts and offers on the makeup products on purchase of the apparel in the store
Additionally, driving up sales from the apparel division through similar marketing strategies will help raise sales through cross-selling techniques.
Interviewer: Great. We can close the case here. Thank you!

Beauty Lies On The Inside Framework & Recommendations
DECLINING PROFITS OF AN APPAREL STORE
Wise Decision if Additional Revenues > Additional Costs
FINDING THE BREAK EVEN POINT

A: BREAK-EVEN POINT (ONE TIME EXPENDITURE)
Fixed Investment = ₹40,000
S.P. of One Product = ₹1,000
V.C. of One Product = ₹400 + ₹100 = ₹500
Break Even Point Of Sales = F.C./(S.P. - V.C.) = ₹40,000/(₹1,000 - ₹500) = ₹40,000/₹500 = 80 Items

B: ANALYSING VIABILITY (ACCOUNTING FOR THE DAILY OPPORTUNITY COST)
Opportunity Cost = ₹5,000
S.P Of One Product = ₹1,000
V.C. Of One Product = ₹400 + ₹100 = ₹500
Required Daily Sales = Opportunity Cost/(S.P. - V.C.) = ₹5,000/(₹1,000 - ₹500) = ₹5,000/₹500 = 10 Items/Day

Clarifying Questions: Where is the store located? How much space is the makeup outlet going to take? Why only makeup as an alternative?
Brownie Points: Mentioning opportunity cost as one of the fixed costs as it ended up becoming crucial to the case
Keep In Mind: Basics of profitability and the profit function are very useful in unorthodox cases like this. Try to incorporate concepts you have studied about before.

Our product is one that would be consumed by families as a whole and not one that is individually purchased by every member of the household (eg. Phones). So, we divide the rural population by the average family size.
Next, we estimate the percentage of rural families that have connection to municipal water supplies and whether this access is throughout the day or during parts of the day. We arrive at the total number of families that would require a product like this. We shall now divide the remaining families into different income groups. The reason for doing this is that on an average, every family would require around 30 litres of water every day, for drinking and cooking. This would mean the purchase of 3 sachets every day. Thus, they use up a box in 4 days. This comes up to approximately Rs. 70 per family in a month. Some families will not be able to afford such an expenditure on cleaning water every month and hence we need to rule them out.
Out of the remaining families, we can assume an average of 3 sachets every day, multiplied into 365, divided by the box size of 12 sachets, to give us the annual market size of approximately 685 crore boxes.
Keeping in mind the availability of certain substitutes and the fact that we might not be able to capture the entire market on arrival, we can estimate around 25% (170 crore) to be captured by us in the first year. Under manufacturing, we need to decide whether we want to import from Germany or manufacture it within the country. Manufacturing within the country not only reduces transportation and import costs but also develops trust since it is made in India.
Under distribution outlets, we need to ensure that our product is available in most kirana shops and small-scale markets as this is the primary point of access to rural families.
Under staff, we need competent people to make the product. More importantly, we would require ground-level salesmen to sell the product in the poorest parts of India.

We can market the product through a variety of ways: Radio, Melas, Village panchayats and billboards. We need to keep in mind that usual methods of marketing such as TV would not be applicable in this case.
Lastly, we need to ensure we have a proper system in case customers have any grievances or queries regarding the product.

Apart from this, I'd like to look at risks that we may face.
Primarily, the biggest risk would be getting rural families to accept the product. There will also be risks of new competitors entering the market. Ensuring that our product performs as promised would be very important as there would be a lot of legal barriers to develop such a product.

title: Schindler's Fit
prompt:
Schindler, a European giant, has recently merged with Voltas, the previous market leader, which is now left with only 2% market share. Decide on a post-merger branding strategy for the newly incorporated company from the following options:
1) Air India-Vistara model: complete acquisition by Air India, and only its name continues in the market.
2) Vodafone Idea model: both brands merge their names into the new company, Vodafone Idea.
3) Tata-JLR model: Tata, Jaguar, and Land Rover have their own cars, but all operate under the same parent company.

notes.title: Questions
items: Branding objective
Product differences
Regional or segment dominance
Financial or time constraints

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Separate brands only when segments differ
Compare each model on revenue vs cost

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Splitting market by city tier
Applying a diversification lens
Spotting premium-dilution risk

framework:
Candidate: Thank you for the case. Before I dive in, I'd like to ask a few questions to understand the problem statement better.
Interviewer: Sure, please go ahead.
Candidate: What is our objective with this branding strategy? Are we trying to maximise revenue, expand reach, or maximise profits?
Interviewer: We are looking to maximise both revenue and profitability.
Candidate: Understood. Are there any product differences or core competencies that set the two brands apart?
Interviewer: For this case, assume that the products sold by both brands are identical.
Candidate: Got it. In India, brands usually target specific regions or consumer segments. For example, Blinkit has a stronger presence in northern India, while Zepto has greater penetration in western India. Does the merged company show any regional dominance in terms of its customer base?
Interviewer: Great question. Schindler primarily operates in Tier-1 (T1) cities through outlets such as Vijay Sales, Croma, and Reliance Mart, owing to its premium brand perception. Voltas, on the other hand, operates mainly in Tier-3 (T3) cities.
Candidate: That distinction is helpful. Are there any financial or time constraints I should keep in mind?
Interviewer: None.
Candidate: Perfect. I'll approach this in two parts. First, I'll lay out my initial hypothesis on which of the three models is likely to work best. Then I'll test it by analysing each model on its revenues and branding costs to see which one is most profitable.
Interviewer: Yes, go ahead.
Candidate: Let me start with the qualitative evaluation of the three models. Starting with the Air India-Vistara model: here, Air India had a substantially larger market share and brand recognition in India, so it could fully absorb Vistara and continue under its own name. That logic does not hold for us. Schindler is a new brand that has just entered India, and Voltas is left with only a 2% market share. Neither brand is dominant enough to absorb the other, so I would strike off this first model.
Interviewer: Fair point. Continue.
Candidate: Next, the Vodafone Idea model, where both names are merged into one. In my opinion this is not the best fit either. Schindler carries a premium perception while Voltas carries a non-premium perception, and the two operate in different markets. If we merge them, it creates confusion in the minds of customers. The upper class will no longer see Schindler as a luxurious product once the Voltas name is attached to it, so the premium positioning of Schindler gets diluted. At the same time, we still won't be able to charge a premium from the middle class because that market is price-sensitive.
Interviewer: So why does the third option avoid that problem?
Candidate: Because the third model, the Tata-JLR model, keeps the brands separate under a common parent. The reason Tata and JLR operate separately is that they cater to different market segments. Jaguar and Land Rover serve the rich, while Tata sells cars like the Tiago or Nano that are tailor-made for the lower and middle classes. We have a very similar situation with Schindler and Voltas, where one is premium and T1-focused and the other is mass-market and T3-focused. So operating separately under the same parent company is the best strategy here.
Interviewer: I really appreciate your approach. Now move on to the profitability analysis for these three cases. For simplicity, consider only branding costs.
Candidate: Perfect, let me go case by case. In the first model, where Schindler becomes the sole brand and Voltas is discontinued, the revenue potential is limited. The focus would shift entirely to the T1 cities, letting go of all the revenue that could be earned from the T3 cities. The cost would sit in the middle range, since only one brand needs to be marketed, but it has to be marketed effectively because Schindler has only just entered the Indian market.
In the second model, the merged brand, revenues would likely be the lowest, because the new company is diluted across both T1 and T3 cities. The middle class would find the new product expensive and might switch to other alternatives in the market, while premium consumers may hesitate to pay a higher price for a brand now associated with a mass-market perception. The cost, on the other hand, would be the highest, because the company would need to invest heavily in repositioning and in resolving the brand confusion in the market.
In the third model, where both brands operate separately, revenues would likely be the highest, because both brands play independently in their respective markets. We also avoid keeping all our eggs in one basket. The cost would still be high, since both brands have to be marketed separately, which is the main drawback of this model.
Considering both revenue potential and branding costs together, the third model, the Tata-JLR approach where both brands operate independently under a common parent company, is the one most likely to maximise profitability.
Interviewer: We are thinking on the same lines. Good work on the approach. We can end the case here.

Candidate: Understood. I'd lay out the strategy as a three-step, sequential approach, where each step builds on the previous one and we proceed only if the previous step is viable. First, financial feasibility: whether domestic manufacturing makes economic sense compared to imports. Second, operational feasibility: whether we can realistically set up a domestic, end-to-end value chain. Third, the policy, compliance, and risk ecosystem: whether there are any regulatory or execution risks that could derail the strategy. Does this approach work, or am I missing anything?
Interviewer: This is a very exhaustive approach and covers everything relevant. Go ahead.
Candidate: I'll start with financial feasibility. The objective is to check whether the delta from domestic production is positive compared to importing EV batteries. I'd break it into three components: revenue per unit, variable cost per unit, and capital expenditure (CAPEX). If domestic production generates higher long-term value than imports across these components, that justifies moving to the next step. Moving to operational feasibility, I'd map the entire EV battery value chain from start to end to identify bottlenecks, breaking it into three stages: raw material procurement; manufacturing, testing, and technology; and distribution and reverse logistics. After evaluating each stage, we can judge whether the ecosystem can be built domestically in a reliable and scalable manner.

Candidate: Within raw material procurement, I'd look at two sources: domestic mining of the key raw materials required for EV batteries, and recycling, especially chemical recycling, since EV batteries are well suited to circularity and recycled materials can be reused as inputs. Within technology and manufacturing, three parts: research and development, covering in-house research, technology development, and acquisition of the required intellectual property (IP); testing, including both early-stage testing and late-stage quality and safety testing; and production and storage, covering the actual manufacturing of batteries and appropriate storage conditions after production. Within distribution and reverse logistics, last-mile distribution to original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and any reverse logistics for defective units or end-of-life batteries.
Interviewer: Very comprehensive. You mentioned CAPEX under financial feasibility. What would you cover there?
Candidate: I'd look at CAPEX across three categories: human capital costs, physical capital costs, and miscellaneous costs such as insurance, marketing, and other supporting expenditures.
Interviewer: Focus on physical capital costs. What would you include?
Candidate: Within physical capital costs, three key components: land and infrastructure costs; plant and machinery costs; and ecosystem enablers' costs, including licensing, IP-related costs, and environmental compliance costs such as waste management and recycling infrastructure.
Interviewer: This is very comprehensive and covers exactly the strategy I wanted you to focus on. With this, we can close the case.

Candidate: For organic growth, I'd break revenue into three levers:
Organic Revenue = Number of Cars × Spare Parts per Car × Price per Spare Part
One quick check before I go deeper: should we also look at increasing the number of cars sold, since more cars on the road directly increases the demand for spare parts?
Interviewer: That's a good observation, but the client is only the spare parts division. So let's focus there.
Candidate: Understood. I'll set the number of cars aside and focus on increasing the number of spare parts sold per car and the price per part. To go deeper, I'd look at our two routes to market separately: the product channel and the service channel.
Interviewer: Let's start with the service channel.
Candidate: Sure. In the service channel, customers come to us directly to get their cars serviced, and we fit our own spare parts during that service. I'd split this channel into two routes: a Direct-to-Consumer route, or D2C, where we deal with the end customer, and a Business-to-Business route, or B2B, where we work with other businesses. Let me start with the Direct-to-Consumer route. I'd think about it in two stages: before the customer buys the car, and after they own it. Before the purchase, there are two opportunities. First, mandatory fitments that are built into the car automatically, for example a spare tyre. At the moment of buying the car, an extra 4,000 to 5,000 rupees for these fitments feels small to the customer, so they rarely object. Second, optional add-ons that the customer can choose to include.
Interviewer: And after the purchase?
Candidate: After the purchase, I'd offer one free service or one free repair along with the car. Customers usually hesitate to visit the official service centre at first. A free first service brings them in, lets them experience the quality of our work, and makes them far more likely to return to us when a real issue comes up later.
Interviewer: You keep mentioning a value proposition. What is the biggest pain point that would push a customer towards a local retailer instead of us?
Candidate: The biggest pain point is price sensitivity. Local retailers are usually cheaper.
Interviewer: So how would you counter that price sensitivity?
Candidate: We can't simply undercut the retailers, because we offer a better service and genuine original parts, so our costs are higher. Instead of cutting the price, I'd raise the value proposition. Many customers, especially price sensitive ones, buy their cars on an Equated Monthly Instalment, or EMI. If we can find a way to fold the cost of their servicing and spare parts into their existing EMI, the value proposition improves a lot. For example, if a local retailer charges 5,000 rupees, our service might cost 10,000 rupees. Paid upfront, that gap feels large. But spread across the monthly EMI, it becomes a small increase of perhaps a hundred rupees a month, which makes our higher quality option feel far more affordable.
Interviewer: Alright. Let's move to the Business-to-Business route within the service channel.
Candidate: In the Business-to-Business route, the key questions are how we sell to our partners and how we get them to prefer us. I'd set up an incentive and milestone program. We define clear milestones, and partners who reach a certain volume of sales or service earn better terms and advantages. The strongest performers can be recognised as our authorized partners. This works as a win-win. Customers get the trust of seeing an official authorized partner badge, so they are comfortable going there. For the retailer, becoming an authorized partner means more business, because customers of our brand will prefer to come to them. And for us, sales rise as more service and parts flow through this partner network.
Interviewer: Good. Can you summarise the case for me?
Candidate: Certainly. Our client is the spare parts division of an automotive OEM that wants to double its revenue in 2 to 3 years. We focused on organic growth and set inorganic growth aside, since our parts only fit our own cars. Within organic growth, we concentrated on selling more spare parts through two channels. In the service channel, on the Direct-to-Consumer side, we capture value before purchase through mandatory fitments and optional add-ons, and after purchase through a free first service that builds trust, supported by EMI bundling to overcome price sensitivity. On the Business-to-Business side, we use a milestone based incentive and authorized partner program to grow sales through our partner network.
Interviewer: That's a clear summary. We can close the case here.

Parts and Recreation Framework & Recommendations
GROWTH STRATEGY TO DOUBLE REVENUE FOR AN AUTOMOTIVE SPARE PARTS DIVISION
Clarifying Questions: Meaning of OEM Channels in play (product and service) Whether the parts fit other cars Top line or bottom line Target and time frame
Brownie Points: Defining OEM before proceeding Bundling service cost into the EMI Building a milestone based authorized partner program
Keep In Mind: Grow parts per car, not volume Raise value instead of cutting price
RECOMMENDATIONS: [FLAG] No recommendation in source material. This was an open-ended, conversational growth case; the interviewer closed it after the structure and summary without asking for a final recommendation.

title: Dry Hard
prompt: Your client is a washing machine manufacturer that has witnessed a steady decline in revenues. Diagnose the problem and give your recommendations.

notes.title: Questions
items: Value chain stage
Market structure
Top-load vs front-load

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Explore external and internal factors
Match product features to local utility costs

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Clarifying competitor product differences
Reframing the drought into a marketing message

framework:
Interviewer: Your client is a washing machine manufacturer that has witnessed a steady decline in revenues. Diagnose the problem and give your recommendations.
Candidate: Sure. Before I lay out my approach, I would like to ask a few preliminary questions.
Interviewer: Certainly, go ahead.
Candidate: To start, which stage of the value chain is the company involved in? And what has been the quantum of this decline, and over what period?
Interviewer: The client is solely involved in the manufacturing of washing machines. The company has witnessed a 20% decline in revenues over the past 1 year.
Candidate: Got it. Should I look only at the revenue side, or has the client also seen any change in costs?
Interviewer: There has been no change in costs. Just focus on revenues.
Candidate: Understood. I would break revenue into two levers:
Revenue = Number of Units Sold × Price per Unit
Have we seen a recent change in either of these?
Interviewer: The number of units sold has gone down. There has been no change in the price.
Candidate: I will further subdivide the factors affecting the number of units sold into three categories: production capacity, distribution, and consumer pull. Have we seen any recent change in the production capacity of the company?
Interviewer: Not really.
Candidate: And has there been any recent change in the distribution of our washing machines?
Interviewer: No.
Candidate: That leaves consumer pull as the likely driver. Should I proceed with that?
Interviewer: Yes, go ahead with consumer pull.
Candidate: For the drop in consumer pull, I see three possible reasons: quality, marketing, and externalities. Am I missing any major factor?
Interviewer: No, you can proceed.
Candidate: Before I examine each one, could you tell me what the market competition looks like?
Interviewer: The market is fragmented, with multiple competitors each holding roughly 15% market share, including our client.
Candidate: Got it. Is our washing machine different in quality from the competitors'?
Interviewer: Yes.
Candidate: I would break quality into four sub-factors: features, after-sale services, maintenance cost, and power requirements. Is any of these different from the competitors'?
Interviewer: Our client's washing machine is smaller in size than the competitors', and is a top-load model, unlike most competitors who have a front-load model. Maintenance cost and after-sale services are the same.
Candidate: My knowledge of washing machine models is limited. Could you elaborate on the difference between top-load and front-load?
Interviewer: A top-load model generally requires more water per cycle than a front-load model.
Candidate: Understood. Moving on, has there been any recent change in the client's marketing strategies?
Interviewer: Nothing as such.
Candidate: Finally, have there been any recent externalities that may have hit consumer pull?
Interviewer: Yes. The nearby region has been struck by drought in the last year.
Candidate: That ties everything together. Our washing machine is smaller in size, so it can wash fewer clothes at once and requires more cycles than the competitors'. On top of that, since the region has been hit by drought, water is scarce and more expensive. So running our machine costs the customer more water and more money than running a front-load competitor's machine, which is why consumer pull has dropped.
Interviewer: You've identified the problem correctly. What corrective action do you recommend?
Candidate: One quick check before I give my recommendations: is it feasible for the client to change the size and type of the washing machine without much expenditure?
Interviewer: That change is likely to be very expensive.
Candidate: Alright. Can I take a couple of minutes to put my recommendations together?
Interviewer: Sure.
Candidate: I would split my recommendations into short-term and long-term.
Short-term:
1) Reduce the price of the washing machines and offer attractive discounts to customers, until the effects of the drought ease off and water availability improves. This will bring down the cost of running our machine and help regain lost sales in the interim.
2) Issue advertisements showing how the water used in the washing machine can be re-used in daily household chores, to mitigate the loss of sales caused by the drought.
Long-term:
1) Improve the company's goodwill in the market by making donations and providing supplies to areas affected by the drought, alongside other Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives.
I think employing these actions can help in improving the company's revenues.
Interviewer: Sounds great. We can close the case here.

Dry Hard Framework & Recommendations
DIAGNOSING A 20% REVENUE DROP AT A WASHING MACHINE MANUFACTURER
Clarifying Questions: Value chain stage Market structure Top-load vs front-load
Brownie Points: Clarifying competitor product differences Reframing the drought into a marketing message
Keep In Mind: Explore external and internal factors Match product features to local utility costs
RECOMMENDATIONS: Short-term: 1) Reduce prices and offer discounts until drought eases and water availability improves. 2) Run advertisements showing how washing machine water can be re-used in household chores to mitigate sales loss. Long-term: 1) Improve company goodwill through donations and supplies to drought-affected areas and other CSR initiatives.

title: Net Worth
prompt: Your client is the Prime Minister's Office (PMO). You are advising the ministry on a vision-setting and economic planning exercise. The brief is to identify sectors where the government should double down on economic policy, with three primary objectives in mind: GDP, private sector investment, and employment. The government has already identified a few sectors and would like your help in confirming whether those choices are prudent.

notes.title: Questions
items: Quantitative targets per objective
Budget or regulatory constraints

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Tie every metric directly to a stated objective
Long horizon elevates sustainability as a separate lens

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Citing twelve nautical miles for territorial waters
Choosing supply-side because exports matter on an island
Applying agricultural consolidation to fisheries

framework:
Interviewer: Your client is the Prime Minister's Office (PMO). You are advising the ministry on a vision-setting and economic planning exercise. The brief is to identify sectors where the government should double down on economic policy, with three primary objectives in mind: GDP, private sector investment, and employment. The government has already identified a few sectors and would like your help in confirming whether those choices are prudent. Please go ahead.
Candidate: Thank you. Before I lay out my approach, I have a few clarifying questions.
Candidate: What is the time period we are looking at for this policy?
Interviewer: Fifteen years.
Candidate: Are there any quantitative targets in mind for the three objectives?
Interviewer: Not really.
Candidate: Are there any budget constraints or regulatory limitations?
Interviewer: No, none. Treat the budget as unrestricted.
Candidate: You also mentioned a few pre-identified sectors. Could you share those along with the rationale?
Interviewer: We will come to that in the latter part of the case. For now, walk me through how you would approach identifying the right sectors.
Candidate: Sure. I will map the economy first, then describe how I would shortlist against the three objectives. I would split the economy into three categories: Primary (agriculture and non-agriculture), Secondary (manufacturing and non-manufacturing), and Tertiary (IT-based and non-IT-based services). I would then assess each sector against three parameters: 1) Current trends, 2) Growth potential over the fifteen-year horizon, and 3) Sustainability — how likely the sector is to remain relevant fifteen years out (kept separate from growth potential because a sector that could be displaced by Artificial Intelligence or automation would score poorly here even if its growth potential looks strong today). I would walk each sector across the three objectives using these parameters, and shortlist the ones that score consistently.
Interviewer: That works. Here are the sectors we have shortlisted so far: Primary — coffee, fruits (oranges and coconuts), fisheries; Secondary — food processing; Tertiary — tourism, Business Process Outsourcing / Knowledge Process Outsourcing (BPO/KPO).
Candidate: Got it.
Interviewer: Based on this list of seven or eight sectors, how would you narrow it down to two or three? What Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) would you use?
Candidate: Let me list the metrics first: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of the sector, employment percentage it accounts for, private sector investment flowing in, startup growth percentage (a leading indicator of investment), a risk or sustainability score, and comparables — sectors in other countries at a similar economic stage in the past and the growth trajectories they followed.
Interviewer: This feels quite cluttered. Remember, you are presenting to a political audience. Simplify it.
Candidate: Fair point. Let me re-organise the metrics directly against the three objectives. GDP: contribution to GDP, GDP growth rate. Private sector investment: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Foreign Institutional Investment (FII), startup growth percentage. Employment: current employment trends, and the risk of human labour being displaced as technology and capital become more abundant in the sector.
Interviewer: That works. Running these metrics, we have drilled down to fisheries as the sector to focus on. It is currently highly underdeveloped and has substantial scope for further growth.
Interviewer: I would now like you to perform a guesstimate: estimate the market size of the fisheries sector in this country. One clarification — the country is not India. It is an island nation in Southeast Asia.
Candidate: Understood. Market size of fisheries can be approximated as number of fishes × average price per fish.
Interviewer: For this exercise, restrict yourself to the number of fishes. Pricing is not what we are testing.
Candidate: Got it. Two broad approaches: demand-side (fishes consumed within the country) or supply-side (fishes harvested or cultivated). The demand-side approach assumes no fish is exported, which is unlikely for an island economy, so I would lean towards supply side.
Interviewer: Agreed. Exports are meaningful here, so demand side is too restrictive. Go with supply side.
Candidate: Before I dive in, how are fishes typically caught in this country? Labour-intensive or capital-intensive? Any advanced technology in use?
Interviewer: No advanced technology. Fishing is largely traditional, through hand and net by local fishermen.
Candidate: That helps. Three possible bottlenecks could constrain the supply side: 1) fishermen, 2) total stock of fishes available, and 3) distributors moving the catch onward.
Interviewer: Focus on the fishes angle. Assume all fishes within the country's territory can be cultivated, so you are estimating the total potential stock irrespective of fishermen, boats, or distributors.
Candidate: Understood. I would first split the country's water bodies into inland and marine.
Interviewer: Assume no fishes in inland water bodies. Focus only on marine.
Candidate: Sure. To estimate the marine area, I would need the country's size and shape.
Interviewer: Land area is 200 km².
Candidate: Two simplifying assumptions: the country is roughly a square island (a 200 km² square gives a side of approximately 14 km), and the ocean surrounds the island on all four sides with fishing possible on all four coasts. One important constraint: a country's fishing rights typically extend only up to its domestic territorial waters, which under international convention is around twelve nautical miles from the coast. Beyond that, fishing requires separate permissions.
Interviewer: Sharp insight. For this case, assume the cultivable marine zone extends 8 km from each coastline.
Candidate: Got it. The outer boundary of the cultivable zone is then a larger square with a side of 14 + 8 + 8 = 30 km. Outer area = 900 km². Subtracting the land area of 200 km², the cultivable marine zone works out to 700 km².
Interviewer: Good. Within this 700 km², fish density is not uniform. How would you think about it?
Candidate: My hypothesis: density is higher closer to the coast (reef and shallow-water habitats) and falls as you move further into the open ocean.
Interviewer: Directionally yes, though the order is slightly different. Moving outward from the coast: Medium-density band — 25 km² (first stretch from coast); High-density band — 400 km² (next stretch, most of the catch); Low-density band — 275 km² (outermost stretch). The three together cover the full 700 km².
Candidate: Got it. I will need a yield assumption for each band.
Interviewer: Take the low-density band as 500 kg of fish per km² per month. Use a 2x multiple for medium and 3x for high.
Candidate: So medium = 1,000 kg per km² per month and high = 1,500 kg per km² per month. Working through each band: Low: 275 × 500 = 1,37,500 kg/month. Medium: 25 × 1,000 = 25,000 kg/month. High: 400 × 1,500 = 6,00,000 kg/month. Total potential fish harvest = 7,62,500 kg per month.
Interviewer: Good. That gives us the size of the prize. One final question: what would you recommend to increase the potential of the fisheries sector in this country?
Candidate: I would split the recommendations into two categories: ways to increase the total number of fishes available, and ways to increase the productivity of catching what we already have access to.
To increase the number of fishes available: 1) Partner with friendly neighbouring countries to cultivate in their waters under a shared arrangement. 2) Pursue international approvals or treaties that allow our fleet to fish in selected international waters. 3) Invest in artificial aquaculture and aquaponics farms on land, which decouple supply from the natural marine boundary entirely.
To increase productivity and efficiency: 1) Introduce better technology, machinery, and modern fishing methods to replace the hand-and-net approach. 2) Group individual fishermen into cooperatives or larger fishing units (analogy: consolidating fragmented agricultural plots — scale unlocks shared investment in machinery and technology that an individual fisherman or small boat cannot afford alone).
Interviewer: That covers it well. We can close the case here.

Net Worth Framework & Recommendations
SECTOR IDENTIFICATION FOR 15-YEAR POLICY (PMO ADVISORY)
Clarifying Questions: Quantitative targets per objective Budget or regulatory constraints
Brownie Points: Citing twelve nautical miles for territorial waters Choosing supply-side because exports matter on an island Applying agricultural consolidation to fisheries
Keep In Mind: Tie every metric directly to a stated objective Long horizon elevates sustainability as a separate lens
RECOMMENDATIONS: Increase fish stock: 1) Partner with neighbouring countries to cultivate in their waters. 2) Pursue international treaties to fish in international waters. 3) Invest in land-based aquaculture and aquaponics farms. Increase productivity: 1) Introduce modern technology, machinery, and fishing methods. 2) Group individual fishermen into cooperatives or larger units.

title: Pound for Pound
prompt: Novo Nordisk has launched a product called Wegovy, which is used to accelerate weight loss. An Indian pharmaceutical company wants to venture into this space and has developed a drug similar to Novo Nordisk's. They want to understand the likely size of the market. The candidate must estimate both the price and the market size, given the drug is launched across urban centres in India, is not recommended for people with cardiac issues or seniors above 60, and has no major side effects.

notes.title: Clarifying Questions
items: Units versus monetary market sizing
Eligibility exclusions (cardiac and age)
Geographic scope (urban versus pan-India)
Side effects affecting adoption

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Affordability is the binding adoption constraint
Cosmetic and medical journeys differ structurally

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Proposing three pricing approaches with explicit bounds
Asking about relapse and lifestyle maintenance
Differentiating cosmetic versus medically obese segments

notes.title: Recommendations
items: Anchor pricing on Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and validate with cost-plus and value-based bounds
Target the obesity segment for volume and the cosmetic segment for premium positioning
Run sensitivity tests on the affordability assumption before committing capacity

framework: Interviewer: I have a situation for you. Novo Nordisk has launched a product called Wegovy, which is used to accelerate weight loss. An Indian pharmaceutical company wants to venture into this space and has developed a drug similar to Novo Nordisk's. They want to understand the likely size of the market. Candidate: Before I begin, I would like to clarify a few things. Are we estimating the market size in terms of the number of units, or in monetary terms? Interviewer: We currently do not have information on the price. That is something we would like you to estimate as well, so you will have to estimate both the price and the market size. Candidate: Understood. Since this is a weight-loss drug, I would like to understand which segments of the population are eligible for the drug and which segments it may not be suited for. Interviewer: The drug is not recommended for people with cardiac issues. Candidate: Got it. Are there any age restrictions as well? Interviewer: Yes. You can assume the drug is not recommended for seniors above the age of 60. Candidate: Would it also be fair to assume a lower age cap of 20 years, since children and adolescents may not typically opt for such medication? Interviewer: That sounds reasonable. Let's proceed. Candidate: One more clarification: are we launching this drug in a specific city, or across urban centres in India? Interviewer: Across all urban centres. Candidate: And are there any side effects associated with the drug that may affect adoption? Interviewer: No, you can assume there are no major side effects. Candidate: Great. Let me walk you through my approach. When estimating the market size, I would like to focus specifically on the number of people who would realistically purchase the drug, rather than those who may only be interested in it. Candidate: I will start with the population of India, which I will assume to be 140 crore. Next, I will split this into rural and urban segments, since the drug is only being launched in urban centres. Initially, I would assume the urban population to be roughly 40 crore. Interviewer: Let's take the urban population as 60 crore instead. Candidate: Sure, I will proceed with 60 crore. Candidate: Next, I will apply an income filter, since affordability will be an important factor for a drug like this. Splitting the urban population into four income segments: Lower income 20%, Lower Middle Class 30%, Upper Middle Class 30%, Rich 20%. Given the likely cost of such treatment, I will focus only on the UMC and Rich segments and exclude the rest. That gives us 50% of the urban population, or roughly 30 crore people. Candidate: Next, I will apply an age filter: less than 20 years 25%, above 60 years 5%, target band 20 to 60 years 70%. Applying 70% to the 30 crore gives approximately 21 crore individuals in the eligible age group. Candidate: Now I would like to estimate which segments within this population would actually consider purchasing the drug. Broadly, I see two categories of potential buyers: 1) Health-conscious individuals interested in fitness or cosmetic weight loss. 2) People who are obese or suffering from health conditions related to high weight. Does this two-category split sound reasonable, or would you like me to consider any other buyer profile? Interviewer: That split works well. Go ahead and size each of them. Candidate: Thank you. For the first category, I will assume around 5% of individuals are highly health-conscious. Applied to the 21 crore eligible base, that gives roughly 1.05 crore people as the cosmetic demand pool. For the second category, I will assume roughly 1 in 5 Indians are obese (20%), giving 4.2 crore people as the medical demand pool. Total demand pool approximately 5.25 crore people. Candidate: I believe we should move to pricing, because the actual buyers will depend heavily on affordability. Interviewer: Yes, we can move on to pricing. Candidate: I would like to determine a price range using three approaches: 1) Competitor-based pricing benchmarked against Novo Nordisk's Wegovy. 2) Cost-based pricing (manufacturing cost plus margin) for the lower bound. 3) Value-based pricing based on willingness to pay for substitutes like gym memberships, supplements, diet programs, for the upper bound. Interviewer: Focus specifically on competitor-based pricing. How would you approach that? Candidate: To benchmark, I would like to understand dosage and treatment length. Interviewer: For fitness or cosmetic weight loss, the treatment lasts about 3 months at roughly Rs 50,000 per month. For obesity cases, the treatment is about one year. Candidate: I also wanted to clarify whether there are relapse cases. Interviewer: No, they do not need to repeat the drug cycle, but lifestyle maintenance is required to prevent relapse. Candidate: To close the estimation, I will apply an affordability filter of 20% on the 5.25 crore demand pool, giving 1.05 crore actual buyers: 21 lakh cosmetic buyers (3 months x Rs 50,000 = Rs 1.5 lakh per person) and 84 lakh obesity buyers (12 months x Rs 50,000 = Rs 6 lakh per person). Sizing in rupees: cosmetic segment 21 lakh x Rs 1.5 lakh = Rs 31,500 crore; obesity segment 84 lakh x Rs 6 lakh = Rs 5,04,000 crore. Total addressable market approximately Rs 5,35,500 crore, or about Rs 5.35 lakh crore (roughly $64 billion). The obesity segment dominates because the treatment duration is four times longer. Interviewer: Makes sense. That was a comprehensive analysis. We can end the case here. Pound for Pound Framework & Recommendations MARKET SIZING FOR WEGOVY-STYLE DRUG (INDIAN PHARMA ENTRY) Clarifying Questions: Units versus monetary market sizing Eligibility exclusions (cardiac and age) Geographic scope (urban versus pan-India) Side effects affecting adoption Brownie Points: Proposing three pricing approaches with explicit bounds Asking about relapse and lifestyle maintenance Differentiating cosmetic versus medically obese segments Keep In Mind: Affordability is the binding adoption constraint Cosmetic and medical journeys differ structurally RECOMMENDATIONS: 1) Anchor pricing on Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and validate with cost-plus and value-based bounds. 2) Target the obesity segment for volume and the cosmetic segment for premium positioning. 3) Run sensitivity tests on the affordability assumption before committing capacity.

items: Business and geography
Specs (fleet, capacity, vehicle type)
Breakeven timeline
Operation plan (days and trips)

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Cost-based price is the floor, not the final number
Use a real competing alternative to value the time saved

Variability factor for climatic and landing conditions

framework:
Candidate: Before I dive in I'd like to clarify a few things. First, can I confirm what the business does and where it operates?

Interviewer: Sure. The company runs flying taxis between Chennai's main airport and two or three points across the city. Think of it as a premium service for people who want to skip road traffic.

Candidate: Got it. Next, the specifications of the E-Plane. Fleet size, seating capacity, and the type of vehicle.

Interviewer: We have a fleet of 7 planes. Each one seats 5 passengers, and the vehicle is essentially an electric drone.

Candidate: Understood. And the goal of the pricing strategy. By when does the company want to break even?

Interviewer: In 3 years. That's the horizon we're working with.

Candidate: Last clarification. Is there a predetermined operation plan? Days per week, and number of trips per day?

Interviewer: Yes, the team has locked that in. 7 days a week, 10 trips a day.

Candidate: That gives me what I need. The approach here is straightforward. There are two cost components, fixed and variable, and the minimum price to charge is the one that lets the business recover both within 3 years.

On the fixed side, two heads:
1. Research and Development costs
2. PPE costs, which means Property, Plant, and Equipment, splitting into land and the flight fleet

On the variable side:
1. Operations, mainly energy per trip
2. Repair and maintenance
3. Labour, both skilled and unskilled
4. Any miscellaneous costs

Does this split look reasonable, or should I consider any other cost head?

Interviewer: That covers it. Start with fixed costs. You can take R&D cost as 4 crore rupees.

Candidate: Noted. For PPE, fleet cost dominates. Let me build up the cost of one E-Plane first. I'd think of it as the cost of an average 5-seater car plus the modules needed to make it airborne.

A 5-seater car is around 10 lakh rupees. The airborne modules are frame, rotors, and electrical circuitry, in a ratio of 1:3:2.

1. Frame: 6 lakh rupees
2. Rotors: 18 lakh rupees
3. Electrical circuitry: 12 lakh rupees
4. Module total: 36 lakh rupees

Thus, cost per plane that comes to 10 lakh plus 36 lakh, which is 46 lakh rupees. I'll round to 50 lakh per plane.

Fleet Cost = 50 lakh * 7 = 3.5 crore rupees

Adding land into the PPE bucket, total fixed cost lands at around 10 crore rupees.

Interviewer: Take that as the fixed figure. Walk me through variables.

Candidate: For operations, energy cost per trip uses the following formula:

Energy Cost per Trip = Distance * Consumption per km * Variability Factor * Cost per Unit Energy

I added a variability factor because for a plane, climatic and landing conditions can move energy consumption significantly trip to trip.

Interviewer: How would you pick the two or three points the plane operates between?

Candidate: Since docking and refuelling happen at the airport, one end of each route is fixed. For the other end, I'd select places that either take a long time to reach from the airport by road, or are inaccessible by road. That's where this service creates the most time-saved value.

Interviewer: Who's actually willing to pay for that?

Candidate: It's a premium service, so the customers will mostly come from the upper strata. Two segments stand out: wealthy residents and tourists.
